newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hospital giant hit by widening federal probe.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hospital giant hit by widening federal probe.

text.p: As federal agents expand their probe of Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp., the nation's largest for-profit hospital company is becoming a symbol for a growing campaign against Medicare fraud and abuse.
Wall Street analysts expect that the investigation could last 18 months or longer and may eventually force the company, based in Nashville, Tenn., into an expensive settlement with the government.
"We're going to be into mid-1998 to get this thing complete. This is a huge investigation," said Jeffrey Villwock, a health care industry analyst at Robinson-Humphrey Co., a brokerage in Atlanta.
"Columbia could be the poster child for Medicare fraud and abuse and that's not a good thing," Villwock said.

The federal probe comes as Congress turns its attention to reforming Medicare, the federal health care programme for the elderly. In a report issued on Thursday, federal authorities said the government overpaid hospitals, doctors and other health care providers last year by $23 billion, or 14 percent of the money spent in the standard Medicare programme.
By going after alleged fraud and abuse in Medicare, legislators hope to reduce the amount they will be forced to cut from the program's budget, analysts said.
"They're going after the largest players because they're the easiest targets and it's a very strong message that's sent," said John Eade at Argus Research Corp. in New York.

Federal agents have visited Columbia/HCA facilities in six states -- Florida, Texas, Tennessee, North Carolina, Oklahoma and Utah -- and seized records related to laboratory billing and home health care operations, Columbia said earlier this week.
Seizure of files reportedly spread on Thursday to the offices of an Atlanta accounting firm that has done billing work for Columbia/HCA. The accounting firm could not be reached for comment.
The investigation, launched in April, has taken a toll on Columbia/HCA stock, which fell another $1.375 to $31.875 on the New York Stock Exchange, down from about $38 on Monday.

The company, with sales of $19.9 billion last year, runs 342 hospitals, 150 surgery centres and more than 570 home health locations in 36 states, England, Switzerland and Spain. The company has 250,000 employees.

Headed by the hard-driving Richard Scott, Columbia/HCA was founded in 1988 and has acquired hospital chains once owned by Humana Inc., the former Hospital Corp. of America and others. Columbia/HCA has focused on wringing higher profits and savings from a notoriously inefficient industry.

"I don't think Columbia has intentionally or systematically tried to defraud the government. I think they've tried to figure out how to maximize their (Medicare) reimbursement within the rules," said Joel Ray at Wheat First Butcher Singer, a brokerage in Richmond, Va.

The company said it had no indication of how long or how deep the federal investigation may extend, but analysts said they expected a long ordeal during which Columbia stock will remain under pressure.
"It's going to be stuck between $30 and $40 a share for a while," Ray said.
The impact of the investigation, while limited thus far, could spread, analysts said.

"You have to wonder -- at what point does this investigation begin to impact morale at the facilities," said Robinson-Humphrey's Villwock. "Or when do insurers or HMOs start to decide something funny is going on and they'd rather not refer patients over there," he said, adding there were no signs that was occurring so far.
